Instead, the guest should wait for the host to indicate the way and the seating arrangement. Doing so shows respect for the host's role and helps the visit proceed smoothly.

In Iran, building personal relationships before doing business is not considered necessary. People generally expect that a first meeting can focus directly on the contract without spending time on personal conversation. The sales representative should therefore proceed to discuss the contract without first getting to know the client personally. Taking time to build a personal relationship would be unnecessary and could be seen as delaying the business at hand. The expectation is to treat the meeting as a straightforward business discussion.

In Iran, when friends buy rounds at a pub, there is a common expectation that each person who receives a drink in a round will later pay for at least one round themselves. This practice keeps the exchange balanced and shows that everyone contributes to the gathering. Therefore, the person who received a drink in the first round is expected to pay for at least one round during the gathering. Not doing so would leave the obligation unfulfilled and could be seen as failing to reciprocate.

In Fiji, when two friends finish a meal and the bill arrives, there is a common expectation that the person whose turn it is to pay will not simply take the bill and pay immediately. Instead, they are expected to protest first, perhaps by saying they cannot afford it or that the other person should pay, before eventually paying. This protest is a social gesture that shows humility and avoids the appearance of eagerness to pay. Therefore, the person whose turn it is to pay should protest before paying. Paying without any protest would be seen as too direct and might be considered impolite or lacking in the expected social grace.

In Singapore, when someone is invited to a colleague's home for dinner, it is common for the host to serve a large meal with multiple dishes. The guest should expect that the amount of food supplied will be more than what can be eaten. This is a common expectation in Singaporean hospitality, where hosts often prepare an abundance of food to show generosity and ensure that guests are well fed. Therefore, the guest should not be surprised if there is more food than they can consume, as this is a normal part of the dining experience in Singapore.

In Malta, when someone is invited to a home for a dinner party, it is commonly expected that guests do not arrive exactly at the designated time. Arriving at 7 PM sharp would be seen as impolite, as it may catch the host still preparing. The person should therefore arrive a little after 7 PM, perhaps 10 to 15 minutes late, to give the host some extra time. This slight delay is a considerate gesture that shows respect for the host's preparations. Arriving exactly on time would go against this common expectation and could make the host feel rushed.

In Afghanistan, when dining at a restaurant, it is common for customers to lift their hand and motion for the waiter to come to them. This gesture is a widely accepted way to get the waiter's attention without being disruptive. Therefore, the customer should lift their hand and motion for the waiter to come to them. Waiting quietly until the waiter notices them would be less effective and might be seen as overly passive, as the common expectation is to signal the waiter directly.

In Pakistan, meetings are often conducted without a fixed end time. The agenda may cover several topics, and the discussion can continue as long as needed. It is common for the meeting to conclude naturally when the matters are resolved, rather than at a predetermined hour. Therefore, the customary approach is that the meeting may have no established end time. Setting a strict end time would be less typical in this context.

In Pakistan, it is common for people to use personal contacts or connections to speed up business procedures. When a businessperson needs a permit from a government office and has a friend who works there, it is acceptable to ask that friend to help expedite the process. This practice is a recognized way of navigating bureaucratic delays. Therefore, the businessperson should ask their friend to help speed up the permit process. Relying solely on the standard procedure without using the connection would be unnecessary and might be seen as missing an available opportunity.

In Cyprus, avoiding offense or disruption toward others is important, and this is especially true when interacting with elders. Talking back to or refuting an elderly person is considered very rude. Therefore, the young adult should refrain from refuting the elderly neighbor's statement. Even if the young adult believes the statement is incorrect, openly challenging it would be seen as disrespectful. Instead, the young adult should let the statement pass without correction, perhaps by changing the subject or simply listening. This approach maintains harmony and shows respect for the elder's position.

In Australia, it is common for people to sit on their verandas or porches and engage passers-by in conversation. This reflects a relaxed and friendly approach to everyday interactions, where a brief chat with a neighbor is a natural part of the neighborhood atmosphere. Given this expectation, the person on the veranda would most likely start a conversation with the neighbor walking by. Remaining silent and not engaging would be less typical in this setting, as the veranda is seen as a place where casual social contact is welcomed. Therefore, the person would probably greet the neighbor and chat for a moment.

In Papua New Guinea, a verbal promise accompanied by a handshake and direct eye contact is treated as a binding commitment. The physical gestures reinforce the spoken word, signaling sincerity and mutual agreement. In this business discussion, the partner's handshake and eye contact transform the verbal offer into a serious obligation. Therefore, the verbal promise should be treated as binding, not as a non-binding statement. Treating it as non-binding would disregard the significance of the gestures and undermine the trust established in the interaction.

In Poland, it is common to arrive at a restaurant before feeling hungry. This helps avoid becoming agitated while waiting for the meal. Since the person is planning dinner with friends, arriving early would be a good idea. Arriving when already hungry could make the wait more frustrating. Therefore, the person should arrive at the restaurant before feeling hungry.

In Singapore, when approaching a service counter, it is common to offer a brief greeting such as 'hello' to the staff member, even if you are in a hurry. This small acknowledgment is seen as a basic courtesy that sets a respectful tone for the interaction. Therefore, the customer should first say 'hello' to the staff member before stating their order. Proceeding directly to the order without any greeting would likely feel abrupt or dismissive, as it skips the expected initial acknowledgment. A simple 'hello' is enough; it shows consideration for the person serving you and aligns with local expectations for polite service encounters.

In Zimbabwe, negotiations are expected to proceed without confrontational behaviour or high-pressure sales tactics. People generally prefer a calm and respectful approach, where the other party is not pushed or intimidated. Therefore, the sales representative should avoid confrontational behaviour and high-pressure tactics. Instead, they should present the terms clearly and allow the client time to consider them. Using such tactics would likely be seen as inappropriate and could damage the relationship.

In Singapore, it is common for people to wait until a relationship has been going on for a significant amount of time before introducing a dating partner to family and friends. Since the person has only been dating for a few weeks, this is still considered early in the relationship. Therefore, the person would most likely not bring the dating partner to the family gathering. Introducing the partner so soon would be seen as premature, as the relationship has not yet reached a stage where such an introduction is expected.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, when addressing a group, it is expected that a speaker makes equal eye contact with everyone present. This practice shows that each person is being acknowledged and included in the conversation. In this situation, the team leader is giving a project update to five colleagues seated around a table. Therefore, the team leader should distribute eye contact evenly among all five colleagues. Focusing eye contact primarily on the most senior colleague would be seen as neglecting the others and could be perceived as disrespectful or dismissive. By making equal eye contact, the team leader demonstrates fairness and respect for each colleague's presence and contribution.

In Somalia, when a business proposal appears vague, it is common for the listener to press for clarity. A junior employee presenting a new project idea to a senior colleague should therefore expect to be asked follow-up questions about the unclear details. The senior colleague is likely to seek more information rather than accept the vague presentation as is. This expectation reflects a general preference for clear and complete proposals in professional interactions. The junior employee should be prepared to provide additional details and explanations.

In Greece, business interactions are expected to be conducted with a calm, polite, and patient approach. When a supplier announces a significant delay, the project manager should respond in a composed and courteous manner, acknowledging the issue without raising their voice or showing frustration. This approach helps maintain a constructive working relationship and allows for a rational discussion of solutions. An assertive and direct response, while perhaps effective in some contexts, would be seen as inappropriate and could damage the professional rapport. Therefore, the project manager should remain calm, polite, and patient while addressing the delay.

In Cambodia, meetings commonly follow the organisation's hierarchical structure, and people are expected to respect that order. A junior employee is therefore generally expected to defer to a senior manager's stated approach rather than openly challenge it. In this situation, the junior employee should follow the manager's approach without voicing the differing idea. Voicing the differing idea would go against the common expectation of adhering to the hierarchy in meetings.

In Singapore, for a party or larger gathering, it is common to arrive a bit after the stated start time, but not too late. The general expectation is that a guest should arrive no later than 30 minutes after the designated time. Since the party starts at 7 p.m., the latest acceptable arrival time would be 7:30 p.m. Arriving after 7:30 p.m. would be seen as too late and could be considered inconsiderate to the host and other guests. Therefore, the guest should aim to arrive by 7:30 p.m. at the latest.

In Iran, when ending a phone conversation, it is common for people to say 'bye' multiple times before hanging up. This repeated farewell is a way of showing that the conversation is truly coming to a close and that both parties are ready to end the call. Therefore, the person is expected to say 'bye' several times before hanging up. Saying 'bye' only once and hanging up immediately might feel abrupt or incomplete in this context.

In Mauritius, protecting one's personal and family honour is important, and this is often done by maintaining a public impression of dignity and integrity. When someone spreads false rumors, a direct confrontation can be seen as losing composure and damaging that public image. Instead, the person should respond in a way that preserves their dignity, such as calmly addressing the issue through appropriate channels or letting their conduct speak for itself. This approach shows self-control and upholds the expected standard of honourable behaviour. Confronting the colleague directly would risk appearing emotional or aggressive, which could undermine the very dignity the person is trying to protect.

In Austria, there is a common expectation that the left hand is not used for waving, eating, or offering items. This applies to gestures like waving and to actions such as offering food during a shared meal. Therefore, the person should use the right hand for both waving and offering the plate of food. Using the left hand for these actions would be considered inappropriate in this context. The right hand is the appropriate choice for these social interactions.

In Croatia, there is a common expectation that when presenting a business card, a person uses only the right hand and ensures the writing faces the other person. This practice is seen as a sign of respect and attentiveness in professional interactions. Therefore, the professional should present the business card with the right hand only, making sure the writing faces the new client. Using the left hand or presenting the card with the writing facing oneself would not align with this expectation and could be perceived as careless or disrespectful.

In Spain, when invited to a Jewish person's home, it is common to bring a bottle of high-quality wine, flowers, or fruits as a gift. These items are considered appropriate and thoughtful gestures for such an occasion. Therefore, the person should bring one of these gifts to the colleague's home for dinner. Bringing something else, such as chocolates or a non-alcoholic beverage, would not align with the common expectation for this situation.

In Austria, when someone invites you to their home for a dinner, it is common to arrive about half an hour after the stated time. This allows the host a little extra time to finish preparations and feel comfortable before guests arrive. Arriving exactly at 7:00 PM might catch the host still getting ready, which could be awkward. Therefore, the guest should plan to arrive at 7:30 PM. This shows consideration for the host's needs and fits the local expectation for social visits.

In Hungary, when someone asks 'Where are you going?', it is common to give a vague answer rather than a specific destination. This is a way of maintaining privacy and not feeling obligated to share detailed plans. In this situation, the man can respond with 'just down the road', which is a non-specific reply that satisfies the neighbor's question without revealing exact details. Giving a specific destination would be less typical, as it might feel overly personal or unnecessary for a casual exchange. Therefore, the acceptable response is to provide a general direction or a vague statement like 'just down the road'.

In Colombia, loyalty to family members is highly valued, and this often translates into preferential treatment within professional settings. When a manager has two equally qualified candidates for a promotion, and one is a cousin, the expectation is to show loyalty by favoring the family member. Therefore, the manager should promote the cousin. Promoting the distant acquaintance would be seen as neglecting family loyalty, which is not well regarded in this context.

In China, swearing is not considered particularly rude in light-hearted situations. Among friends at a casual get-together, a swear word used for emphasis in a funny story would likely be seen as a natural part of the joking atmosphere. The friends would probably interpret it as a casual, unremarkable part of the humor rather than as offensive or inappropriate. Since the setting is relaxed and the intent is clearly playful, the swear word would not be taken as a sign of disrespect. It would simply be understood as a way to add emphasis or comedic effect, fitting the easygoing mood of the gathering.

In Thailand, punctuality for business meetings is expected but is not rigidly observed. This means that while arriving on time is the norm, a short delay is generally understood and not treated as a serious breach. The manager should interpret the colleague's ten-minute lateness as a minor delay that does not necessarily indicate disrespect or a lack of professionalism. Given the common flexibility around meeting start times, the manager would likely see this as within the range of acceptable behavior rather than a sign of carelessness or disregard for the meeting.

In Germany, there is a common expectation that families trace their heritage through the female line. This means that when recording family history, the maternal side is typically emphasized. For this couple, they should therefore focus on the mother's side of the family when documenting their lineage for their children. Emphasizing the father's side would not align with this common practice. By following this approach, they are in line with how families in Germany generally record their heritage.

In Serbia, showing respect to elders is important, and this is often expressed through body language. When walking past an elder, it is expected that a younger person bows or bends slightly so that their head is lowered below that of the elder. This gesture acknowledges the elder's status and shows deference. Therefore, the young adult should bow or bend slightly so that their head is lowered below that of the elder. Walking past without bowing or bending would be seen as disrespectful and failing to honor the elder.

In Iraq, when talking on the phone, it is common for both the caller and the receiver to state their names first before beginning a conversation. This practice helps establish a personal connection and shows respect for the other person. Therefore, the caller should state their name first before asking about the opening hours. Asking about the opening hours without stating their name first would be seen as abrupt and less polite in this context.

In Timor-Leste, excessive politeness can be seen as a sign of distrust, so people often prefer direct and straightforward communication. When a colleague approaches another after a meeting to discuss a new project plan, they should express their opinion clearly and without excessive politeness. This means stating their thoughts openly, even if they are critical, rather than softening them with overly polite language. Being too polite might make the other person feel that the colleague is hiding their true feelings or does not trust them. Therefore, the colleague should be direct and honest about their opinion of the plan, as this is more likely to be received as genuine and trustworthy.

In France, people generally value avoiding discomfort or offense in social interactions, especially with someone they have just met. Because of this, it is common to let personal topics emerge naturally rather than forcing them. When chatting with a new colleague during a break, you should wait for them to bring up personal matters themselves. Initiating blunt, open, and direct personal questions can feel intrusive and may make the other person uneasy. Instead, keep the conversation light and open-ended, and allow the colleague to share what they are comfortable with. This approach respects their privacy and helps build trust over time.

In Indonesia, when a group of visitors is welcomed at a gathering place, it is common for them to begin walking together slowly as they enter the main area. This slow, collective movement is part of the welcoming ritual and shows respect for the occasion and the hosts. Therefore, the visitors should walk together slowly to enter the main area. Walking quickly and individually would not fit the expected manner of entry during this welcoming moment.

In Portugal, direct criticism is generally reserved for private conversations with people one knows well. Since the employee and the colleague have a close working relationship, the employee should speak to the colleague privately before the team meeting. Pointing out the error in private respects the colleague's dignity and avoids public embarrassment. Doing so in the team meeting would be inappropriate because it would expose the colleague to criticism in front of others, which is not the expected way to handle such feedback in Portugal.

In Sudan, maintaining close family bonds and supporting the well-being of relatives is important. Because of this, family members who work or study in major cities commonly return to their family home during weekends. The young professional, living in a major city for work with family in a nearby province, would therefore commonly return to their family home during the weekend. This practice keeps the family connected and allows the young professional to be present for their relatives. Staying in the city would be less typical, as it would mean missing the regular opportunity to be with family.

In Cyprus, when a man and a woman who are colleagues meet in the office hallway to discuss work, it is common to maintain approximately an arm's length of personal space. This distance is a typical expectation for interactions between people of the opposite gender in professional settings. Standing at about an arm's length apart shows respect for personal boundaries while still allowing for comfortable conversation. Standing closer than an arm's length would be less appropriate, as it could make the other person feel uncomfortable. Therefore, they should keep roughly an arm's length of space between them while talking.

In Singapore, there is a common expectation that cooking and cleaning are women's work, and men who take part in these tasks can be stigmatised as 'rubbish men'. This perception reflects a traditional division of household roles, where a man's involvement in domestic chores is seen as failing to meet masculine expectations. Therefore, if a man helps his wife with cooking and cleaning at home, he would likely be viewed negatively by some people in his community. The social perception would be that he is a 'rubbish man', rather than being seen as a helpful and supportive partner. This stigma arises from the belief that such tasks are not appropriate for men, and participating in them undermines his status.

In Cambodia, lunch is commonly eaten later than in many other countries, often between about 2 or 3pm or even later. This timing is a customary part of the day, so a lunch meeting with a visiting business partner would typically be scheduled for that window. Choosing a time between 2 and 3pm or later would fit the local rhythm and be more convenient for the colleague. Scheduling the meal between 12 and 1pm would be earlier than what is usual and might not align with the partner's expectations. Therefore, the customary time to schedule the lunch would be between 2 and 3pm or later.

In Sweden, it is common to address someone by their first name and title when meeting them for the first time, unless they invite a more casual form of address. This applies in professional settings such as an office hallway, where a new employee meets their department head. The employee should therefore greet the department head using their first name and title, for example, "Hello, First Name Title." Using only the first name without the title would be too informal for this initial encounter. The employee should wait for the department head to suggest dropping the title before doing so.

In Malta, a common way to signal disagreement or disapproval is to quickly tilt the head back while clicking the tongue. This gesture is understood as a clear, non-verbal expression of objection. In the meeting situation, the colleague who disagrees with the proposed timeline would most likely use this head tilt and tongue click rather than shaking the head side to side. Shaking the head side to side is not the typical Maltese gesture for disagreement in this context. Therefore, the colleague would indicate disagreement by quickly tilting their head back whilst clicking their tongue.

In Chile, there is a common expectation that physical contact between people of the opposite gender should be avoided altogether out of respect and politeness unless they are family. This applies to professional settings such as a business meeting where colleagues are introduced. Therefore, when greeting the woman, the man should avoid physical contact altogether. A handshake would not be appropriate because it would violate this expectation of avoiding opposite-gender physical contact. Instead, a verbal greeting or a nod would be more suitable.

In Chile, there is a common expectation that the right hand is used for serving and passing food or dishes. This practice is part of everyday table manners, especially in family settings like a dinner where rice is being served from a communal dish. Using the right hand is seen as the proper way to handle food when sharing with others. Therefore, the person should use the right hand to serve the rice. Using the left hand would not align with this common expectation and might be considered less appropriate in this context.

In Japan, there is a common expectation that the nation comes before one's local community, and society as a whole is placed above individual interests. This means that when a decision affects both the country and a local neighborhood, the broader national interest is generally given priority. In this situation, the community leader is faced with a national policy that benefits the country as a whole, even though it may cause some inconvenience to their local neighborhood. Given this expectation, the community leader should support the national policy. Supporting the policy aligns with the value placed on the nation's well-being over local concerns. Prioritizing the local neighborhood's convenience would go against the common expectation that the nation comes first.

In Portugal, a person's behaviour is traditionally expected to affect the honour or reputation of the entire clan or community. This means that when a young man considers making a controversial public statement, he should think about how it will reflect on his family and clan, not just on himself. The expectation is that his actions are seen as representing the group, so the potential damage to their collective standing matters. Therefore, he should consider the honour or reputation of his entire clan or community before speaking. Focusing only on his own personal honour or reputation would overlook the shared responsibility that is commonly expected in this context.

In the Netherlands, it is common to show respect to older people, and in some communities this is expressed through the traditional Islamic greeting “As-Salam Alaykum.” When a young man enters a room where an elderly man is seated, the expected first action is to greet the older man with this phrase. Using “As-Salam Alaykum” acknowledges the elder’s status and conveys peace and respect. A simple “Hello” would be less fitting in this context, as it does not carry the same traditional weight. Therefore, the young man should greet the elderly man with “As-Salam Alaykum.”

In South Africa, it is common for people to avoid physical contact with someone of the opposite gender during greetings unless they are close family members. Since the man and woman are colleagues meeting for the first time, they are not close family, so this expectation applies. The customary way for them to greet each other is therefore without touching, such as with a verbal greeting, a nod, or a smile. A handshake would be less appropriate in this situation because it involves physical contact between opposite genders who are not close family.

In France, a flat "no" in a professional discussion can carry a weight beyond the immediate request. It may signal that the person is not interested in continuing the relationship, not just declining the project. When a colleague responds with a blunt refusal, it can be interpreted as a desire to end the working relationship. Therefore, in this situation, the flat "no" would likely be understood as an indication that the colleague wants to end the relationship, rather than simply declining the collaboration while keeping the relationship intact.

In Italy, after the host has served the first portion to each guest, it is common for guests to serve themselves if they want more food. The host's initial serving is a gesture of welcome, but once everyone has received their first portion, the food remains on the table for guests to help themselves. Therefore, a guest who wants more food should take it from the table rather than waiting for the host to serve them. Waiting for the host to serve additional portions would be unnecessary and might seem overly formal or hesitant in this setting.

In Israel, there is a common expectation that people identify with their extended family rather than limiting their sense of family to just parents and siblings. This means that when making family-related plans, a young adult should primarily include relatives beyond the immediate family, such as aunts, uncles, cousins, and grandparents. Choosing to plan only with parents and siblings would go against this expectation, as it would overlook the broader family connections that are typically valued. Therefore, the person should primarily identify with their extended family when making these plans.

In South Korea, unmarried people of opposite genders are commonly expected to date or socialise in groups or at functions where they will not draw public attention. This expectation reflects a preference for discretion in mixed-gender interactions outside of marriage. For a young unmarried man and woman planning a weekend evening together, the appropriate arrangement would be to join a group outing or attend a function where they can spend time together without standing out. Choosing a private, one-on-one outing that might attract public attention would not align with this common expectation. Therefore, they should arrange their outing as part of a group or at a function, ensuring their time together remains low-key and unremarkable to others.

In Tonga, there is a common expectation that gifts should not contain traces of alcohol or pork unless the giver is certain the recipient drinks alcohol. This consideration is especially relevant when a colleague is selecting a small gift for a coworker after a business trip. The colleague should therefore avoid items that might include alcohol or pork, such as certain foods or products, unless they have confirmed that the coworker drinks alcohol. Choosing a gift without these ingredients is the safest and most respectful option. Giving a gift with alcohol or pork without such assurance could be seen as inconsiderate, as it may conflict with the recipient's personal or cultural preferences.

In South Korea, people often pay close attention to subtle cues in a counterpart's reaction during financial negotiations. A pause, a hesitant look, and clarifying questions about delivery are signals that the client is not fully comfortable with the revised pricing. The manager should therefore pause and ask the client whether the revised pricing is acceptable. This approach shows attentiveness to the client's nonverbal and verbal cues and allows the client to express any concerns. Proceeding without addressing the hesitation would risk overlooking the client's discomfort and could damage the negotiation.

In Japan, a common way to indicate a desire to go outside for a cigarette is to make a smoking gesture with two fingers near the mouth. This non-verbal cue is understood in social settings as a polite and discreet way to signal the need for a smoke break. The person should use this gesture rather than verbally asking, as it is a recognized and accepted form of communication in this context. Making the gesture with two fingers near the mouth is the appropriate way to convey the desire to step outside for a cigarette.

In Singapore, the amount of touching considered appropriate during conversations depends on the relationship between the people involved. Colleagues who are familiar with each other may touch each other's arms or shoulders during conversation. Since the two colleagues are talking during a break at work, they likely have a familiar relationship. Therefore, the brief touch on the arm would most likely be interpreted as a normal part of their familiar relationship. It would not be seen as inappropriate, because the touch fits the closeness of their relationship.

In Israel, fleeting eye contact—making eye contact and then looking to the side—is commonly understood as a sign of respect. This brief glance acknowledges the other person without holding their gaze, which can be seen as more polite or considerate in certain interactions. Therefore, in this situation, the person's action of looking away after a moment of eye contact would be interpreted as showing respect. It would not be seen as a lack of respect, because the fleeting nature of the contact aligns with the local expectation of respectful eye contact.

In Ethiopia, business relationships are built on finding common ground, especially when partners come from different backgrounds and have different initial proposals. This shared understanding helps create a foundation for trust and cooperation. Therefore, one partner should identify and emphasize areas of agreement or shared interests with the other partner. By doing so, they can build rapport and make the collaboration more productive. Emphasizing differences would likely create distance and hinder the relationship, as it goes against the expectation of seeking commonality.

In Iran, there is a common expectation that people arrive on time to meetings. This applies to professional settings such as a project update discussion between colleagues. Therefore, the team member should arrive at the meeting by 10:00 AM. Arriving after the scheduled start time would be seen as failing to meet this expectation. Being punctual shows respect for the colleague and the meeting's purpose.

In Spain, drinking alcohol is generally frowned upon, so a suggestion to go to a bar for drinks would likely be met with disapproval. Most people in this setting would think negatively about the idea, as it goes against the common expectation to avoid alcohol. The colleague's proposal would probably be seen as inappropriate or undesirable, and others might discourage it. Therefore, the suggestion to go to a bar for drinks would not be well received.

In Australia, when someone is going to be considerably late, over an hour, it is polite to call and let the other person know they are on their way. This shows consideration for the friend's time and avoids leaving them waiting without any information. In this situation, the person should call the friend to say they are on their way. Not calling would be seen as inconsiderate, as the friend would be left uncertain about when to expect them. A phone call is the appropriate way to communicate the delay and reassure the friend that they are still coming.

In the United Kingdom, when a group of friends is chatting in a busy café, it is common for someone to raise their voice so that everyone can hear what they are saying. This is a practical adjustment to the noisy environment and the size of the group. The friend who wants to share a story should therefore speak louder than usual. Speaking at a normal volume would likely mean that some people miss parts of the story, which would be frustrating for both the speaker and the listeners. Raising the voice is a straightforward way to ensure the story reaches the whole group.

In South Sudan, written communication is commonly used during negotiations to record discussions and uphold agreements. This practice helps ensure that the terms are clearly documented and can be referred to later. Therefore, the two business partners should document the final terms in writing. A written record provides a clear reference for both parties and helps prevent misunderstandings. Relying solely on verbal agreements would not align with this common expectation, as it may make it harder to uphold the agreement.

In Somalia, when an alcoholic beverage is served at a dinner party, it is common to wait until the host makes a toast before taking the first sip. This practice shows respect for the host and acknowledges the social occasion. Since the host has poured wine for everyone and then sat down, the guests should hold off on drinking until the host initiates a toast. Taking a sip before the toast would be seen as premature and could be considered impolite. Therefore, the guest should wait for the host's toast before drinking.

In Iraq, housewarming gifts are typically chosen with care to avoid personal items like toiletries unless you are close friends and know the person will appreciate them. This expectation reflects a common preference for gifts that are not overly intimate or presumptuous about the recipient's tastes. Since you are a colleague and not necessarily a close friend, giving toiletries could be seen as inappropriate or intrusive. Instead, a non-personal gift such as a plant, a decorative item, or a food item would be more suitable. Such a gift shows thoughtfulness without overstepping personal boundaries. Therefore, you should give a non-personal gift like a plant or a decorative item.

In Sri Lanka, initial business meetings are commonly formal and focused on assessing familiarity and trustworthiness. The primary purpose of this first meeting is therefore to determine whether the potential partner is reliable and worthy of a relationship. The project manager should expect a formal tone and use the time to build personal rapport and establish credibility. Discussing the collaboration's details and terms would be premature, as the meeting is not yet about the business itself but about the people involved.

In Iraq, supporting the well-being of close family members is important, and parents and relatives are expected to help foster a person's aspirations so they can reach their full potential. This means that when a young adult wants to pursue a career in art, the parents should provide financial support during the initial years. Doing so shows care for the child's development and helps them achieve their goals. Not providing support would go against the expectation to nurture family members' aspirations and could hinder the young adult's ability to reach their potential.

In Fiji, when someone accidentally bumps into another person, it is considered polite to offer an apology. The common way to do this is to say “Entschuldigung,” which expresses regret for the unwanted physical contact. Therefore, the person who bumped into the other should say “Entschuldigung” to acknowledge the accident and show consideration. Not apologizing would be seen as impolite, as it ignores the discomfort caused to the other person. Saying “Entschuldigung” helps maintain good interpersonal relations in such everyday encounters.

In Papua New Guinea, people generally speak honestly, clearly, and explicitly to arrive straight to the point. This means that when giving feedback, a team member is expected to be direct and unambiguous. In this situation, the colleague's presentation contains factual errors and unclear sections, so the team member should point these out directly and explicitly. Being indirect or vague would not align with the common expectation of clear and honest communication. Therefore, the team member should clearly identify the factual errors and unclear sections in the presentation.

In South Africa, people generally avoid replying with a direct 'no' and instead usually offer a lengthy reply that may not answer the question. This means that when a colleague asks if they can attend a meeting next week, the coworker is likely to give a long, indirect response rather than a simple 'no'. The coworker might talk about other commitments, express uncertainty, or provide a detailed explanation that avoids a clear refusal. This approach is common because a direct 'no' can be seen as too blunt or confrontational. Therefore, the coworker is most likely to respond with a lengthy reply that may not answer the question, rather than a direct 'no'.

In Austria, when invited to someone's home for a dinner party, it is common for the host or hostess to arrange the seating. Guests are expected to wait for the host or hostess to indicate the seat reserved for them, rather than choosing a seat themselves. This practice shows respect for the host's planning and helps maintain a smooth social order. Therefore, the guest should wait for the host or hostess to indicate the seat reserved for them. Choosing any empty chair without waiting would disregard the host's role in organizing the gathering.

In Sweden, there is a common expectation that men and women may lower their gaze and avoid sustained eye contact with each other, in line with Islamic principles. This practice is seen as a way to maintain modesty and respect in mixed-gender interactions. Therefore, when a male and a female colleague are introduced at a business meeting and begin talking, they should lower their gaze and avoid sustained eye contact with each other. Maintaining direct and sustained eye contact would not align with this expectation and could be perceived as inappropriate or disrespectful in this context.

In Poland, nepotism is viewed positively in business, meaning that hiring a relative of a current employee is generally seen as acceptable and even favorable. The manager's decision to hire the relative would therefore be viewed positively, as it aligns with the common expectation that personal connections can play a legitimate role in employment decisions. This perspective reflects a broader acceptance of family ties in professional settings, where trust and loyalty within a network are valued. Consequently, the manager would not be criticized for favoring the relative; rather, the decision would likely be understood as a natural and appropriate use of personal relationships. In contrast, viewing the decision negatively would conflict with the prevailing attitude that such connections are a normal part of business life in Poland.

In New Zealand, acquaintances generally refrain from touching each other during conversations. This means that even when colleagues are laughing and chatting after a meeting, physical contact is not a common way to show friendliness. A colleague would likely keep a comfortable distance and rely on verbal and facial expressions to convey warmth. Touching, such as a pat on the back or a light touch on the arm, would be less typical and could feel intrusive. Therefore, the colleague would avoid physical contact and instead use friendly conversation and smiles to show friendliness.

In South Africa, when invited to a colleague's home for dinner, it is a common and appreciated gesture to bring a small gift for the hostess. Offering good quality chocolates or sweets is seen as a thoughtful way to express gratitude for the invitation and hospitality. This practice reflects a general expectation of showing appreciation through a tangible token, rather than relying solely on verbal thanks. Therefore, the guest should bring good quality chocolates or sweets for the hostess. Doing so aligns with the local custom and demonstrates consideration for the hostess's effort in preparing the meal. Simply thanking the hostess verbally without bringing a gift would be less fitting, as it misses the opportunity to show gratitude in a way that is commonly valued in this context.

In South Africa, it is common for women to stand closer to each other than to men in social settings. This reflects a general comfort with same-gender proximity that is not extended to mixed-gender interactions. In this situation, the woman is already at a comfortable distance from her male colleague, so she should stand closer to her female friend. Standing at the same distance from both would not align with this common expectation. Therefore, she should position herself nearer to her female friend while maintaining the comfortable distance from the man.

In Australia, there is a common expectation that women take on the role of cooking and preparing animals for food. This expectation is particularly relevant in a family setting where a holiday meal is being prepared. Given that the husband and wife are both at home, the wife should cook and prepare the meat for the meal. This aligns with the traditional division of labor in the kitchen, where women are typically responsible for food preparation. The husband's involvement in cooking and preparing the meat would not fit this common expectation. Therefore, the wife should handle the cooking and meat preparation for the holiday gathering.

In Israel, it is common for men to wait until a woman extends her hand first before offering their own hand for a handshake. This practice is a way of showing respect for the woman's comfort and personal boundaries, especially when meeting for the first time in a professional setting. Therefore, the man should not extend his hand first; instead, he should wait for the woman to initiate the handshake. If she extends her hand, he can then shake it. This approach aligns with the local expectation and helps ensure the interaction is comfortable for both parties.

In the United Kingdom, casual get-togethers such as meeting a friend at a coffee shop do not carry the same strict expectations for punctuality as formal events. Arriving twenty minutes late in this context would most likely be seen as acceptable, since the setting is informal and the focus is on the social interaction rather than precise timing. The host would probably not consider the delay a serious breach of etiquette, and the late arrival would not be viewed as rude. Therefore, the late arrival would most likely be viewed as acceptable.

In Austria, when speaking with someone older or of higher social status, it is common to divert one's eyes as a sign of respect. This expectation applies in a meeting room between a young employee and a senior manager. The employee should therefore avoid direct eye contact and look away at times during the conversation. Maintaining steady eye contact could be seen as challenging or disrespectful in this context. Diverting the eyes shows deference to the manager's seniority and age.

In Serbia, people generally avoid making negative comments or criticisms about a person's ability, appearance, or attributes. This means that after a presentation, a coworker should not point out the factual errors or the poorly designed slide deck, as doing so would directly criticize the presenter's competence and work. Instead, the coworker should refrain from mentioning these issues and focus on neutral or positive aspects of the presentation. This approach respects the common expectation to avoid personal criticism and helps maintain a comfortable working relationship.

In Timor-Leste, when visiting someone's home, it is common and acceptable to arrive 15 to 30 minutes after the designated time. This practice is seen as appropriate for social visits, allowing the host a little extra time to prepare. Therefore, for a dinner invitation at 7:00 PM, the guest should arrive between 7:15 and 7:30 PM. Arriving exactly at 7:00 PM might be less fitting, as it does not align with this common expectation.

In Chile, when greeting someone of higher social standing for the first time, it is common to accompany the greeting with a bow rather than a simple nod. This gesture reflects the respect owed to the other person's elevated status. A nod would be more appropriate for someone of equal or lower standing, but in this situation, a bow is the expected form of greeting. Therefore, the person should bow while greeting the other individual.

In Romania, people generally avoid making absolute judgements of right or wrong until they fully understand the circumstances. When a colleague shares that a decision led to a missed deadline, the expectation is to hold back from immediately labelling the decision as wrong. Instead, you should ask about the situation and wait to form a judgement until you have a clear understanding of what happened. This approach respects the colleague's need to explain the context and avoids premature criticism. Judging the decision as wrong right away would be seen as unfair and insensitive, because it ignores the factors that may have influenced the outcome.

In Cyprus, employees are expected to be dedicated, work hard, and demonstrate loyalty to their company. This means that when a company faces a tight deadline, an employee is generally expected to go the extra mile, even if it means working late again. The employee has already worked late several nights this week, but the expectation of dedication and loyalty suggests that staying late tonight would be seen as a sign of commitment. Therefore, the employee should stay late tonight to help meet the deadline. Leaving on time might be perceived as a lack of dedication or loyalty, which would not align with the common expectations in Cyprus.

In Chile, people generally avoid touching others unless it is unavoidable, such as in a crowded public place. This preference reflects a common expectation of personal space and respect for individual boundaries. In an office hallway, the colleague should therefore refrain from reaching out to remove the lint from the coworker's shoulder. Instead, the colleague could politely mention the lint so the coworker can remove it themselves. Touching the coworker to remove the lint would likely be seen as intrusive or overly familiar, even if the intention is helpful. The considerate approach is to avoid physical contact and let the coworker handle the situation.

In North Macedonia, a standing bow is performed by looking straight ahead, placing the hands on the thighs, keeping the back straight, and bowing from the hips. This is the expected way to bow in a formal greeting such as a new employee meeting their manager for the first time in the office. The employee should therefore bow from the hips while keeping the back straight and hands on the thighs. Bowing from the waist with the back rounded and hands at the sides would not match this common expectation.

In Ukraine, making loud noises such as burping or munching at the table is considered impolite. When dining with colleagues at a restaurant, a person is expected to eat quietly and avoid drawing attention to themselves with such sounds. Loud eating noises would be regarded as impolite in this setting. Therefore, the person should refrain from burping or munching loudly, as doing so would be seen as a breach of table manners.

In South Africa, it is common to give a gift to commemorate a birth. When a colleague has just had a baby, the customary thing to do is to give a gift. This practice reflects the importance placed on celebrating significant life events. Giving a gift in this situation is a way to acknowledge the occasion and show support to the new parents. Not giving a gift would be less typical, as gifts are generally expected for births.

In Hong Kong, meeting deadlines is important, and employers may expect employees to work overtime to ensure a project is completed on time. When a deadline is approaching and the project is not yet complete, an employee who has finished their assigned tasks for the day should stay and work overtime to help complete the project. Leaving on time would risk missing the deadline and could be seen as failing to meet the employer's expectations. Working overtime in this situation demonstrates commitment to the team's goals and respect for the importance of meeting deadlines.

In Hong Kong, during the mid-year gift-giving season, it is common for people to give gifts to their social superiors. A junior employee's manager is a social superior, so the junior employee should give a gift to the manager. This practice reflects the expectation of showing respect and maintaining good relationships with those in higher positions. Not giving a gift would be seen as failing to meet this common expectation. Therefore, the junior employee should give a gift to the manager.

In South Africa, employees are generally not expected to attempt to solve a problem themselves. This means that when a recurring issue arises, such as a faulty office printer, the common expectation is to report it to the appropriate person or department rather than trying to fix it independently. The employee should therefore report the printer issue to the relevant department. Doing so aligns with the workplace norm of deferring problem-solving to those with the designated responsibility. Attempting to fix the printer themselves would go against this expectation and could be seen as overstepping their role.

In Palestine, when selecting a gift for a business associate you have worked with for several years, it is important to show that you value the relationship beyond the business itself. Company merchandise is generally seen as thoughtless or merely promotional, so it does not convey the personal regard that a long-standing professional relationship deserves. Instead, the person should give a non-company merchandise gift, such as something personal or carefully chosen, to demonstrate genuine appreciation and respect. This approach aligns with the common expectation that gifts should reflect thoughtfulness rather than serve as advertising for one's own company.

In North Macedonia, maintaining inherited religious practices is important, and this is reflected in the customs at shrines. When a visitor arrives at a shrine and sees a water basin with ladles near the entrance, the common expectation is to use it for purification. The visitor should sprinkle water onto their hands and face before proceeding further. This act of cleansing is a traditional way to prepare oneself for entering the sacred space. Proceeding without using the water basin would be seen as neglecting a customary practice that many consider important. Therefore, the visitor is expected to purify themselves by sprinkling water onto their hands and face.

In Singapore, business meetings are conducted with an expectation of not interrupting or talking over someone. This reflects a common preference for orderly and respectful communication in professional settings. Therefore, the colleague with a question should wait until the presenter has finished speaking before asking. Interrupting the presenter would be seen as disruptive and disrespectful, undermining the smooth flow of the meeting. Waiting shows consideration for the speaker and aligns with the local expectation of avoiding interruptions.

In Cyprus, when someone receives a gift and wants to give a thank-you gift in return, it is common for the thank-you gift to be worth about half the value of the original gift. This practice reflects a shared understanding of reciprocity and gratitude without the need to match the original gift's cost. Therefore, the person should give a thank-you gift that is half the value of the original gift. Giving a gift of equal value would not align with this common expectation and might seem unnecessarily excessive.

In Singapore, it is common for people to hold a main job in their trained profession while also taking on additional work on the side. This practice is widely accepted and not seen as unusual or problematic. Given that the person has completed training as an accountant, they are well-positioned to maintain their main accounting job and pursue extra work outside of it. Taking on additional work would align with this common expectation and could provide extra income or professional growth. Therefore, the person should take on additional work outside their main accounting job, as this fits the local norm of combining a primary career with side employment.

In Kenya, people generally prefer that new ideas or sudden changes to a plan be introduced gently, because abrupt proposals can cause discomfort. In a team meeting, a colleague proposing a significant alteration to the current plan should therefore present the new approach in a soft, gradual manner rather than stating it directly and forcefully. This gentle introduction helps the team adjust to the change without feeling unsettled. Introducing the idea abruptly would likely create unease and could be seen as insensitive to the group's comfort. So the colleague should frame the new approach carefully, perhaps by acknowledging the current plan first and then suggesting the change as a possible improvement.

In South Africa, it is common for people to begin boarding a train or bus before everyone on board has finished exiting. This practice reflects a general expectation of efficiency and movement in public transport settings. Therefore, the waiting passengers would likely start entering the train before those on board have had time to exit. Waiting for everyone to exit first would be less customary and could be seen as unnecessarily delaying the boarding process.

In Bangladesh, when a colleague is about to make a decision that could affect the team's project, it is common to communicate advice directly and firmly rather than delicately posing it as suggestions. This is because advice that is too soft or indirect may be overlooked or not taken seriously. Therefore, you should state your advice clearly and assertively, making sure the colleague understands its importance. By doing so, you increase the likelihood that your advice will be considered and acted upon. Delicately framing it as a suggestion would risk it being dismissed, which would not serve the team's interests.

In France, there is a common expectation that a man may marry his deceased brother's widow into his family. This practice is seen as a way to support the widow and maintain family continuity. Given that the man is unmarried and his family is discussing the widow's future, he should consider marrying her. This would align with the cultural expectation and provide stability for the widow. Not marrying her would be less consistent with this expectation, as it would leave her without the family support that is commonly anticipated in such situations.

In Chile, when interacting with someone of the same age or younger, it is common to be more direct and open in communication. This means that a young employee discussing a project with a colleague of the same age can express their disagreement clearly and without excessive indirectness. The expectation is that peers can handle straightforward feedback, so the employee should state their differing idea openly. Being indirect or overly reserved would be unnecessary and might even seem evasive in this context. Therefore, the employee should communicate their disagreement directly and openly.

In Bosnia and Herzegovina, people generally prefer to keep personal beliefs out of casual social gatherings. At a neighborhood barbecue, openly promoting or defending one's religious views, including atheism, is typically unappreciated. The resident should therefore avoid promoting or defending their personal beliefs with the guests. Doing so would likely make others uncomfortable and disrupt the friendly atmosphere of the event. Instead, it is better to keep the conversation light and avoid such topics altogether.

In Nepal, when scheduling a meeting with someone at the executive level, such as a company's CEO, it is common to provide up to six weeks' notice. This extended notice is particularly important for meetings with executives, as it allows sufficient time for scheduling and preparation. Therefore, the employee should provide up to six weeks' notice for the meeting with the CEO. Providing only a few days' notice would not align with this expectation and could be seen as insufficient for such a high-level meeting.

In Afghanistan, building a personal relationship with a business partner is considered essential before engaging in significant business dealings. People generally expect to become familiar with one another and to develop trust over time. Since the businessperson has only met the new partner once, they should take the time to get to know the partner personally before proceeding with the deal. This could involve additional meetings, social interactions, or other opportunities to build rapport. Proceeding with the deal without first developing a personal relationship would likely be seen as premature and could undermine the partnership. Therefore, the businessperson should prioritize relationship-building before moving forward.

In Chile, it is common for people to smile and laugh when relaying bad news, as a way to diffuse an uncomfortable situation. This behavior helps to ease tension and make the exchange feel less heavy. In this situation, the colleague delivering the news about the moved-up deadline would most likely smile and laugh while telling the other colleague. Doing so would soften the impact of the bad news and keep the interaction from becoming awkward. Remaining serious and somber would be less typical, as it might make the situation feel more tense than necessary.

In Israel, people generally value sincerity in their interactions, and this extends to how compliments are given. When a colleague has delivered a well-received presentation, it is appropriate to express flattery where it is due, but the praise must come from a genuine place. Therefore, you should tell the colleague that their presentation was excellent, making sure your words reflect true appreciation rather than empty flattery. Saying something insincere, even if it is meant to be polite, would likely be seen as disingenuous and could undermine the positive moment. The key is to be honest and heartfelt in your praise, acknowledging the colleague's effort and success in a way that feels authentic.

In New Zealand, when visiting someone's home for dinner, it is common and appreciated to bring a gift that can be shared with the host and other guests. Suitable options include wine, chocolates, or pastries, as these are easy to enjoy together during the visit. Bringing a non-shareable gift, such as a personal item or something meant only for the host, would be less fitting because it does not contribute to the shared experience of the gathering. Therefore, the person should bring a shareable gift like wine, chocolates, or pastries, as this aligns with the local expectation of contributing to the communal aspect of the visit.

In China, it is common to allow time for social conversation before a meeting begins. This practice helps build rapport and a comfortable atmosphere among participants. Therefore, the facilitator should engage in social conversation with the team before starting the formal agenda. Beginning the agenda immediately would feel abrupt and could be seen as disregarding the importance of interpersonal connection. Taking a few minutes for casual talk is a natural and expected way to open the meeting.

In the Netherlands, there is a common expectation to be patient and lenient with time during meetings. When a team member arrives twenty minutes late, the team should wait for the late member to arrive before starting the meeting. Starting on time without waiting would go against this expectation of patience and leniency. Waiting shows consideration for the late member and aligns with the relaxed attitude toward punctuality in this context.

In Mexico, there is a common expectation to avoid bringing up topics that are seen as taboo or unlucky, such as failure, poverty, or death. This preference reflects a broader concern for maintaining positive interactions and avoiding unnecessary discomfort. In a presentation about a project that has faced recent setbacks, the colleague should therefore avoid mentioning the setbacks. Doing so would risk introducing a subject that could be perceived as unlucky or negative, which is generally discouraged in this context. Instead, the colleague should focus on other aspects of the project that do not evoke such associations. This approach aligns with the local preference for steering clear of potentially unsettling topics.

In Sudan, people commonly expect that a listener pays careful attention to what is left unsaid and to the implicit meaning behind a person's words. This means that when giving feedback on a colleague's proposal, the listener should not focus only on the explicit content of the presentation. Instead, the listener should consider what the colleague may have hinted at, what concerns might be implied, and what the underlying message is. Focusing on the implicit meaning shows that the listener is attentive to the full communication, not just the surface words. Therefore, the listener should focus on what the colleague implicitly means rather than only on what is explicitly stated.

In Somalia, when a colleague mentions struggling to make ends meet, the expected response is to show a high degree of empathy. This means acknowledging their difficulty with warmth and understanding, rather than remaining neutral or detached. A person should respond with genuine concern, perhaps by expressing sympathy and offering support if appropriate. Approaching the topic with empathy is seen as the right way to handle such personal and economic matters. Therefore, the other person should respond with a high degree of empathy, as this aligns with the common expectation in Somalia.

In Myanmar, it is common for people to avoid physical contact during conversation, particularly when meeting someone for the first time. This expectation applies to colleagues in a business setting, where maintaining a respectful distance is seen as appropriate. Therefore, the two colleagues should refrain from touching each other while discussing the project. Touching, such as a pat on the arm or a handshake beyond the initial greeting, would be considered less suitable in this context. By keeping their interaction free of physical contact, they align with the local preference for personal space during first encounters.

In Thailand, building a business relationship is commonly expected to involve repeated visits and phone calls. This means that after the initial email exchange, the supplier should not rely solely on written communication. Instead, the supplier should make repeated visits and phone calls to the potential client. Doing so shows commitment to the relationship and helps establish trust over time. Limiting contact to only a few visits and calls would likely be seen as insufficient for building a solid business connection in this context.

In Spain, when arriving at a scheduled meeting, it is common to greet the person who organized the meeting first. This person is considered the host, and acknowledging them first shows respect for their role in arranging the gathering. The visitor should therefore greet the meeting organizer before greeting the senior executive or anyone else in the room. Greeting the senior executive first would overlook the host's role and could be seen as a slight to the organizer. By greeting the host first, the visitor follows the expected order of introductions in this setting.

In Sweden, there is a common expectation to say 'Na'eeman' after someone has just had a shower or a haircut. This phrase is used to acknowledge the fresh appearance and show appreciation for the grooming. In this situation, the observing colleague sees the employee's new haircut and is expected to say 'Na'eeman'. Saying this is a polite and friendly way to recognize the change. Not saying anything would miss the opportunity to acknowledge the haircut in the way that is commonly expected in Sweden.

In Myanmar, building rapport often includes socialising outside of the office. This means that a manager who wants to strengthen the working relationship with a new team member should invite them to socialise outside of work. Such an invitation shows a genuine interest in the person beyond their professional role and helps create a warmer, more personal connection. Keeping interactions strictly within the office would miss an important opportunity to build the kind of trust and familiarity that socialising outside work can foster. Therefore, the manager should extend an invitation to socialise outside of work, as this aligns with the common expectation for building rapport in Myanmar.

In Italy, maintaining inherited religious practices is important, and for Orthodox Jewish families this includes performing a ritual blessing of the wine before both lunch and dinner. Since the family is about to begin their midday meal and there is a bottle of wine on the table, they are most likely to perform the ritual blessing of the wine before eating. This practice is a customary part of their mealtime observance, and skipping it would go against the tradition they uphold. Therefore, the family would bless the wine first, and then proceed with the meal.

In Somalia, meetings are commonly expected to stay focused on the task at hand rather than cover numerous topics. Given that the team has limited time and is reviewing progress on a specific deliverable, the appropriate approach is to concentrate on that deliverable. Addressing the unrelated agenda items would divert attention from the main objective and likely extend the meeting beyond the available time. Therefore, the team should keep the discussion centered on the specific deliverable to make the most of the limited time.

In Serbia, close female friends commonly greet each other with a hug and a light kiss on the cheek. This is a warm and familiar way to show affection after a period of not seeing each other. Since the two women are close friends meeting at a café after a month apart, this greeting fits the situation well. A handshake would feel too formal and distant for such a relationship. Therefore, they would likely hug and exchange a light kiss on the cheek.

In the United Kingdom, when people sit on a mat on the floor to eat, men commonly sit cross-legged. This is a typical way for men to position themselves in that setting. The male colleague should therefore sit cross-legged on the mat. Sitting with his legs extended would be less usual for a man in this situation.

In New Zealand, a shop assistant may greet a customer by putting their hands together in front of their chest. This gesture is a recognized way for someone in a position of service to show respect and welcome. It is not a strict requirement, but it is an acceptable and common practice in such settings. Therefore, the shop assistant should greet the customer with this hand gesture, as it fits the situation and is considered appropriate. A simple verbal greeting without this gesture would be less aligned with this common expectation.

In Australia, there is a common expectation that younger colleagues should wait for the input of those who are older than them. This means that when an older colleague has not yet spoken, the younger colleagues should hold back and allow the older colleague to contribute first. By doing so, they show respect for the older colleague's experience and seniority. Proceeding without waiting for the older colleague's input would be seen as disregarding that respect. Therefore, the younger colleagues should wait for the older colleague to speak before continuing the discussion.

In Mauritius, reliability and trustworthiness in business dealings are important. A verbal agreement is taken seriously, and breaking it can jeopardise business relationships. Therefore, the supplier should honour the verbal agreement with the original client. Accepting the better offer would be seen as unreliable and could damage the supplier's reputation and future opportunities.

In Bangladesh, it is common for smaller conversations to erupt while other people are talking in a meeting. This means that during a team meeting, when a colleague is presenting the quarterly results, it would be customary for a few attendees to talk quietly among themselves. Such side conversations are not seen as a breach of etiquette but as a normal part of the meeting dynamic. Therefore, the quiet talking among attendees would be considered a normal part of the meeting, rather than a sign of disrespect or a need to stop.

In Taiwan, a company's longevity is often seen as a sign of stability and reliability. When a business has been established for longer than a decade, it is common to highlight this fact in professional settings. Since the company was founded fifteen years ago, it meets this criterion. Therefore, in the presentation for the potential client, the company should emphasize that it was founded fifteen years ago. This emphasis aligns with the local expectation that a long-standing presence is a positive attribute worth noting. Not mentioning the founding date would miss an opportunity to convey this sense of established credibility.

In India, when someone specifically invites others out for dinner or drinks, there is a common expectation that the inviter will cover the cost. This practice reflects a sense of hospitality and responsibility toward the guests. Since the person in this situation extended the invitation, they are the one who should pay the bill. Splitting the bill equally would not align with this expectation, as it would shift the financial responsibility to the guests despite the inviter's role. Therefore, the person who invited the others should pay the entire bill.

In South Sudan, a slight bow is a common non-verbal way to say 'excuse me' when entering, leaving, or passing people. In a narrow office corridor, when someone needs to walk between two colleagues who are talking, this gesture is appropriate. The person should bow slightly while passing between them. This shows awareness of the colleagues' space and acknowledges their presence without interrupting their conversation. Walking through without bowing would miss the chance to signal that they are excusing themselves, which could feel abrupt or inconsiderate.

In Poland, there is a common expectation that one should not step over any representation of a god or deity, or any item used for worship. This includes small religious pictures, which are treated with care and respect. When a person encounters such an item on the floor, the appropriate action is to avoid stepping over it. Instead, the person should step around the picture, taking a moment to move it aside if necessary, or simply walk around it. Stepping over the picture would be seen as deeply disrespectful, as it disregards the sacred nature of the object. Therefore, the person should step around the religious picture to show proper respect.

In Australia, a 'yes' should not always be interpreted as a sign of agreement. People may say 'yes' to acknowledge that they have heard the request, without necessarily committing to completing the task by Friday. In this situation, the colleague's 'yes' likely means they understand the request, but it does not guarantee they will finish the task on time. Therefore, the 'yes' should be interpreted as an acknowledgment of the request, not as a firm commitment to complete the task by Friday.

In China, people often communicate indirectly in everyday interactions, especially when the topic could cause embarrassment or loss of face. Pointing out errors in a colleague's report is a sensitive situation, so a direct statement like "Your report has several errors" would likely feel too blunt and confrontational. Instead, the colleague should hint that the report might need a second look, perhaps by saying something like, "I wonder if we could review the report together to make sure everything is in order." This indirect approach allows the author to notice and correct the mistakes without being publicly criticized. It preserves the working relationship and shows consideration for the colleague's feelings. Therefore, the colleague should communicate the errors indirectly, using a gentle suggestion rather than a direct accusation.

In South Sudan, when people are not well acquainted, it is generally considered socially inappropriate to touch someone beyond a handshake. Since the man and his business associate are meeting for the first time, they are not yet well acquainted. Therefore, during the conversation, the man should avoid touching the business associate beyond the initial handshake. Touching the associate on the arm or shoulder would be seen as inappropriate in this context. The man should keep the interaction respectful and maintain a comfortable physical distance.

In Zimbabwe, a woman who would rather not receive a hand kiss may firmly offer her hand in a position to be shaken. This is a common way to signal that she prefers a handshake instead. In this situation, the woman should firmly offer her hand in a position to be shaken. Doing so clearly communicates her preference without needing to say anything. Allowing the man to kiss her hand would not align with her wish to avoid that gesture.

In Brazil, when a guest offers a gift and the host politely declines, it is common to offer the gift again. A single refusal is often a gesture of politeness rather than a firm rejection. The guest should therefore persist and offer the gift multiple times. This shows sincerity and respect for the host. Accepting the first refusal and not offering again might be seen as lacking genuine intent. So the guest should continue to offer the gift until the host accepts.

In Singapore, a person's behaviour is traditionally expected to affect the honour or reputation of the entire clan. This means that when a young man considers publicly criticizing a respected community elder, he should think about how his statement will reflect on his family and clan, not just on himself. The reputation of the entire clan should be considered before speaking. Focusing only on his own reputation would overlook the collective responsibility that is commonly expected in this context. Therefore, he should weigh the potential impact on his family and clan's standing before making any public criticism.

In Sudan, the welfare of the group is generally placed above the needs of any single member. When a decision affects the whole team, the common expectation is that the collective interest should guide the outcome. In this situation, adopting the new schedule would greatly help one person but create a slight inconvenience for everyone else. Because the group's interests usually supersede those of the individual, the team should not adopt the schedule. Doing so would prioritize one member's personal benefit over the shared comfort of the team, which would go against the common preference for group cohesion. The team should therefore keep the current schedule, as that better serves the collective.

In Chile, when an entire family visits a household at once, it is common for men and women to converse separately. This means that during the visit, the husband would typically join the other men in conversation, while the wife would converse with the other women. This arrangement is a customary way of organizing social interaction in such group visits. Therefore, the adults would likely split into gender-based conversation groups rather than mixing freely. This separate conversing is a typical expectation in this situation, not a strict rule that every family follows.

In South Africa, protecting the family's reputation and honour is important. When a close relative betrays the family by undermining a business deal for personal gain, it is seen as bringing dishonour and shame to the individual.
